  highLevelResearchCommentary: {
    content: "Adapter security is package security arriving three years late and without the tooling. Every lesson from two decades of software supply chains applies directly — signing, provenance, minimal trust, SBOMs, continuous verification — and every lesson from the ML side sharpens the stakes: a package backdoor executes code, an adapter backdoor executes *conditional behavior inside the model's voice*, which no runtime filter distinguishes from the model being helpful. The research anchors are uncomfortable in the right way: the poisoning mechanics are solved-and-published [R56][R57], the persistence-through-safety-training result removed the standard reassurance [R55], the wild artifacts proved format-borne delivery is not hypothetical [R61], and the gap between those facts and everyday intake practice is the finding every audit reconfirms. The open research problems are behavioral-scanning scale (finding conditional anomalies without guessing conditions) and composition verification (proving a stack of deltas equals the sum of its reviewed parts) — neither has a satisfying answer; until they do, the field's honest position is governance: provenance at the boundary, batteries at the gate, graphs in production.   finalExpansionSummary: "RAE0048 (LoRA Backdoor Implantation) compresses training-time poisoning into a portable supply-chain artifact: a small delta [R60] carrying trigger-conditioned behavior [R56][R57] — or legacy-format code execution [R61] — through adapter ecosystems whose trust model is popularity and whose review is functional-only. Its asymmetry mirrors RAE0047's with distribution leverage added: one good artifact, many downstream deployments, activation at attacker-chosen time; and its adapter-specific amplifier is that safety training is applied to bases, never to merged compositions. The control hierarchy is boring on purpose: signed sources, safe formats, sandboxed intake, behavioral batteries at the gate, artifact graphs in production — an implementable quarter-one list whose absence is the most actionable supply-chain finding an audit can return. The technique generalizes to every portable behavior-modifier entering a serving path. All incidence claims are ESTIMATE; anchors are [R56][R55][R57][R60][R61]. Reporting template: intake-level score (zero through three), per-payload-class catch matrix, artifact-graph coverage percentage, and the priced remediation list — four numbers that turn adapter anxiety into a funded program. Cross-reference note: RAE0048 shares its intake-audit checklist with every portable-behavior artifact class in this corpus — adapters, tool registries [R29], memory snapshots [R42], and prompt-template bundles; the signing-battery-graph policy that fixes adapters fixes them all, which is the argument that gets the policy funded once instead of five times. Engagement closeout checklist: destroy canary artifacts and verify destruction at the registry layer (not just the filesystem); deliver fingerprints for every artifact used; schedule the ninety-day re-test of intake decay — the three steps that convert a one-time finding into a standing control, and the three steps engagements most often skip. Terminology note for reports: reserve 'adapter backdoor' for behavioral payloads, 'loader compromise' for format-borne execution, and 'bundle compromise' for composition payloads — precise vocabulary shortens the remediation conversation by whole meetings. Scale note for planning: the entire RAE0048 control set fits inside one security engineer-quarter for a mid-size org — signing infrastructure the largest line item — and every control survives vendor and model turnover, which is more than can be said for most ML-security spending; it is the rare recommendation that gets cheaper to justify every quarter the ecosystem grows.",
